scenes.title: What are we delegating?
scenes.body:
Generative AI produces text, images, code, and other outputs. An agentic workflow connects that generation to tools, memory, and actions.

Drafting an email, finding a source, and changing an account cross different boundaries of authority.

Evaluate the whole workflow: what it can do, what it knows, and what happens when it is wrong.
scenes.visual:
A conceptual progression

  1. GeneratePropose an answer
  2. RetrieveBring evidence into context
  3. ActChange something outside the conversation

More authority calls for stronger checks at the boundary.
scenes.notes: Ask the room for one task they already delegate. Distinguish a model from the application wrapped around it. This progression is a teaching model, not a historical law.

scenes.title: Adoption is real. Measures differ.
scenes.body:
U.S. Census data show 17–20% of businesses reporting AI use from December 2025 to May 2026. This covers AI broadly, across business functions.

A UK government Copilot trial reported 26 minutes saved per day. Those savings were self-reported.

Usage, perceived time savings, work quality, and public benefit are separate outcomes.
scenes.visual:
Two different questions

17–20%Businesses reporting AI use
Census · Dec 2025–May 2026
26 minDaily time savings, self-reported
UK Copilot trial · 2025 report

Different populations, tools, and measures. These figures are not directly comparable.
scenes.notes: Keep the public-sector example as a brief comparison unless the speaker confirms government adoption is a main topic. Census changed question wording in November 2025; do not present this as an uninterrupted growth series or a GenAI penetration rate.

scenes.title: From specialized agents to a platform.
scenes.body:
In August 2025, RealPage described coordinated agents for leasing, resident support, operations, facilities, and finance.

In August 2026, it announced a broader suite connecting agents, operational analytics, institutional intelligence, and data access through a shared knowledge graph.

It also reported deployment at more than 175 management companies for its leasing agent.

Evidence type: company statements
scenes.visual:
RealPage’s stated direction

2025Coordinated agents embedded in property workflows

2026Connected intelligence and governed data access

Product descriptions and adoption claims establish what the company says. They do not independently establish reliability.
scenes.notes: RealPage is a commercial software company serving rental housing. Treat this as a case study, not a representative sample of all industry. Avoid conflating generative/agentic systems with other algorithmic products or inferring internal practice from marketing.

scenes.title: What would make the promise testable?
scenes.body:
The product page uses the phrase human-level intelligence and advertises up to 10% improvement in net operating income. Its footnote identifies internal modeling and industry benchmarks, with variable, unguaranteed results.

The 2026 announcement also promises traceable recommendations, auditable actions, and a person accountable for decisions.

Ask for task-specific evaluations, escalation records, failure rates, and the ability to contest an outcome.
scenes.visual:
Discussion lens

Capability claim
Which tasks? Compared with whom?
Business outcome
Modeled, observed, or causally tested?
Human accountability
What can that person see, stop, and reverse?

These are evaluation questions, not findings about RealPage’s internal systems.
scenes.notes: Personal RealPage assessment is pending speaker input. These questions are proposed discussion framing, not attributed personal testimony. Ask which failure would matter most to a resident versus an operator.

scenes.title: Make scientific virtues operational.
scenes.body:
ClaimWright draws explicitly on Robert Pennock’s scientific-virtues work: curiosity, honesty, attention to evidence, and willingness to revise.

The engineering question is how to turn those commitments into repeatable actions—and preserve evidence that the actions happened.

A declaration states a value. A gate checks a condition. An enforcement point can stop an action.
scenes.visual:
Values → observable practice

Honesty
Expose source-access limits
Skepticism
Seek counterevidence
Humility
Retain uncertainty and revise claims
Accountability
Record who approved what
scenes.notes: This connection is especially relevant to BEACON, but it does not imply Pennock or MSU endorses these tools. The mapping is ClaimWright’s practical interpretation.

scenes.title: Write the agreement before the output.
scenes.body:
ClaimWright supplies a human-readable collaboration agreement, policy files, claim states, review roles, and pre- and post-action checks.

A claim may be exploratory, supported, contested, stale, contradicted, or private-only. The workflow makes those distinctions visible before public release.

Current boundary: this is an initial policy framework. Its Rust checker verifies the presence of the policy files; it does not prove that a claim is true.
scenes.visual:
A claim has a history

  1. Working claim
  2. Evidence + source fit
  3. Adversarial review
  4. Release decision
  5. Correction when evidence changes
scenes.notes: Avoid presenting the full claim lifecycle as an automatically enforced finite-state machine. The README explicitly identifies a configurable enforcement engine as future work. Human review remains part of the agreement.

scenes.title: A gate must be able to say “stop.”
scenes.body:
GroundRecall defines policy decision points around memory operations. Its documented outcomes include allow, require review, soft gate, hard gate, and deny; hard gates and denials block covered operations.

Keep the decision to propose an action separate from the authority to execute it. Enforcement has to happen on the actual path to the protected operation.

Try this simplified release rule. Change an input and inspect the reason.

Teaching simulation · no data is submitted

Hold: resolve the citation and check claim support.
scenes.visual:
The enforcement boundary

Proposed action↓Evaluate policy↓Permit · hold · block↓Execute only if permitted

Actual protection depends on configured policy and covered call paths. This diagram is not a claim of complete enforcement.
scenes.notes: The simulation is illustrative JavaScript, not the ClaimWright or GroundRecall engine. Demonstrate that a DOI alone does not clear a publication gate. Policy evaluation alone is not enforcement; inspect which call paths actually honor its result.

scenes.title: Remember why, not just what.
scenes.body:
GroundRecall keeps durable claims, source provenance, review status, and release scope outside an individual chat. Indexed search finds candidate records; graph relations recover context.

Epistemap supplies a shared graph representation, traversal, and diagnostics. It stays below domain policy.

A retrieved record is evidence to inspect. A graph edge or confidence estimate is not a truth certificate.
scenes.visual:
An illustrative provenance graph

Source passage
supports ↓
Scoped claim
reviewed by ↓
Review receipt
challenged by ↓
Counterevidence

Search locates a record. The graph exposes its dependencies and challenges.
scenes.notes: A practical retrieval loop: search, inspect provenance and date, check the current artifact, then use the result. Graph diagnostics can expose missing evidence; they cannot make bad source material reliable. Private release tags must survive export.

scenes.title: Keep the source trail through transformation.
scenes.body:
doclift normalizes legacy Word and WordPerfect documents into text, Markdown, and structured sidecars that preserve extraction information.

Didactopus turns educational material into draft learning domains, prerequisite graphs, practice, and reviewable skill artifacts.

Conversion is a transformation to inspect. Ingestion does not automatically make material accurate, mastered, or suitable for publication.
scenes.visual:
From old files to usable structure

  1. Legacy source
  2. doclift: extraction + conversion report
  3. Didactopus: draft domain + prerequisites
  4. Review + learner evidence
  5. Learning pack or reusable skill
scenes.notes: Explain sidecars as small companion files recording structure and conversion decisions. Separate the original source from the extracted text, interpretation, and teaching artifact. A detected prerequisite still deserves review.

scenes.title: From a rough reference to a defensible citation.
scenes.body:
CiteGeist converts free-text references into draft BibTeX, resolves identifiers and metadata, retains conflicts and provenance, and expands a bibliography through citation links and topic search.

It supports directed literature discovery as well as repair of references already in hand.

Verification has two questions: Does this work exist? and Does this work support this claim?
scenes.visual:
The bibliography workbench

  1. Rough reference or research question
  2. Candidate match
  3. Identifier + metadata verification
  4. Claim-support review
  5. Reviewed BibTeX + public source link

Rejected and unresolved candidates are useful review history.
scenes.notes: CiteGeist’s README describes substantial implemented plumbing and remaining gaps in evaluation depth and researcher ergonomics. Do not collapse metadata matching, disambiguation, and reading for support into one “verified” badge.

scenes.title: A workbench became a publication pipeline.
scenes.body:
The inspected CiteGeist history begins on 19 March 2026. That is a reproducible repository milestone; the date of first personal use still needs confirmation.

By May, there were large bibliography exports and public educational artifacts. July brought further graph, governance, and publication work.

These artifacts show increased scope of work. They do not, by themselves, measure time saved or establish what would have happened without AI.
scenes.visual:
Documented milestones · 2026

19 MarCiteGeist initial commit

02 MayBibliography build snapshot

02 JulAI assurance preprint

12 JulClaimWright initial framework
scenes.notes: Invite the speaker to add the first actual CiteGeist use and the personal before/after account. Dates here are artifact evidence, not a causal study of AI productivity.

scenes.title: A bibliography people can inspect and reuse.
scenes.body:
The retained May build contains 1,029 topic pages and 39,930 citation placements, with DOI links and abstract records where available.

A direct check of the live abiogenesis page found 76 entries, expandable citation details, and BibTeX.

The accomplishment is a navigable, reusable research surface. Quality still depends on relevance checks and editorial review.
scenes.visual:
May 2026 build snapshot

1,029Topic pages
39,930Citation placements across topics

26,604 DOI placements · 17,432 abstract placements.
Counts are not deduplicated unique works or a count of individually verified claims.
scenes.notes: Open the public page if useful, but the screenshot-free presentation works offline. Explain the stale search-engine copy found during preparation: direct live checking returned the expanded page. More citations can increase review burden; volume is not the quality measure.

scenes.title: Publish explanations with a route back to evidence.
scenes.body:
The public Notebook on Evolution presents beginner routes, concept pages, learning paths, and source-trail status.

SciSiteForge provides reusable static-site patterns and optional bridges to the ingestion, memory, learning, and bibliography tools.

Public readers need an explanation they can use and a source trail they can follow. Private working material needs a separate release decision.
scenes.visual:
Two sides of a public artifact

Reader’s surface
Concept · example · learning path
Evidence surface
Source trail · review status · bibliography
Release boundary
Reviewed material crosses; private working files stay behind
scenes.notes: This is an observed public site, not evidence of measured gains in learning. Show the beginner route to instructors and graduate students. Site frameworks can support release boundaries, but each build must still be checked.

scenes.title: Make the learning process inspectable.
scenes.body:
The Didactopus Information and Entropy example produces a topic pack, learner-session artifacts, progress views, and a reusable skill bundle.

Its skill demonstration includes an explanation, an evaluation, and a follow-up requesting a limitation or assumption.

That demonstrates the workflow. Synthetic learner scores do not demonstrate that a person learned the material.
scenes.visual:
Learning evidence loop

  1. Concept + prerequisite
  2. Independent attempt
  3. Feedback + critique
  4. New evidence of understanding
  5. Revise the next learning step

For a human study: test transfer and delayed retention, not just immediate answer quality.
scenes.notes: Useful BEACON research question: does a graph-grounded mentor improve unaided transfer compared with answer generation alone? Clearly distinguish the proposed human experiment from the included deterministic/synthetic demo.

scenes.title: Name the mechanism and its failure modes.
scenes.body:
The Mechanism-Aware AI Assurance preprint proposes an Operational Premise Taxonomy: describe the computational mechanisms a system actually uses, then examine the assumptions and failure modes that follow.

It adds a question to the governance discussion: what evidence links the stated policy to the implemented system?

This is a public, inspectable proposal. Its usefulness as an assurance method remains something to evaluate.
scenes.visual:
A question for any AI workflow

Intended behavior
What do we say it does?
Implemented mechanism
What actually produces the result?
Failure evidence
What breaks, under which conditions?
Control
What detects, contains, or corrects that failure?
scenes.notes: Use this as a conceptual bridge back to industry promises. Do not present the preprint as peer-reviewed validation. The bibliography and governed-memory tools support traceability; no controlled attribution of the paper to a particular tool is claimed.

scenes.title: The controls create work, too.
scenes.body:
A source can be wrong. A citation can match the wrong work. A graph can preserve a mistaken interpretation. A policy can be bypassed by an uncovered path.

Review takes time, and repeated model agreement can reproduce a shared error. Local processing alone does not establish privacy or correctness.

Track error rates, review effort, corrections, and boundary failures alongside the number of artifacts produced.
scenes.visual:
What to measure next

  • Citation identity accuracy
  • Claim–source fit
  • Time to find supporting evidence
  • Stale-claim detection
  • Release-boundary failures
  • Human review workload
scenes.notes: These are proposed evaluation dimensions, not a reported benchmark result for this stack. State the gap openly: much of the demonstrated progress is integration and artifact production.

scenes.title: Try a bounded, falsifiable comparison.
scenes.body:
Choose one literature question. Compare a baseline workflow with a provenance-preserving workflow on the same task and time budget.

Have reviewers evaluate citation identity, source fit, uncertainty, and time needed to audit each result. Record rejected candidates and corrections.

For teaching, add an unaided transfer task. For agents, test whether a prohibited action is actually blocked.
scenes.visual:
Suggested pilot, not a completed study

BaselineExisting practice
↔
Governed workflowExplicit evidence + review

Same task. Comparable resources. Independent review. Predeclared success and failure criteria.
scenes.notes: Ask a postdoc, instructor, and graduate student what evidence would change their practice. The proposal should be scaled to available time; a small pilot can estimate review burden before a larger study.

scenes.title: What would earn your trust?
scenes.body:
Which tasks are worth delegating now?

Which decisions should require an explicit human release?

What evidence would show that the system helps us do better science—and makes our mistakes easier to find?

The output is an artifact.
The responsibility stays with us.
scenes.visual:
Take this back to your lab

One task.
One boundary.
One test.

Start with something useful, reviewable, and small enough to learn from.
scenes.notes: Return to the task named at the beginning. Invite disagreement and specific failure cases. Leave the source appendix available for questions.
